name: systemctl
summary: Inspect and control systemd services (units): status, start, stop, enable at boot.

install.note: Only on systemd-based systems. Alpine (OpenRC), many BusyBox/Buildroot images (SysV init scripts), WSL1 and most containers do not run systemd; 'System has not been booted with systemd' means exactly that.

compat: Yocto images may use systemd or SysV init depending on DISTRO_FEATURES / INIT_MANAGER. On SysV systems services are scripts in /etc/init.d/.

examples.title: Check a service's status and recent log lines
examples.explain: Read-only; works without root, though some log lines may be hidden.
examples.output: 'Active: active (running)' is healthy; 'failed' shows the exit code. 'Loaded: ... enabled' means it starts at boot. The last few journal lines appear below.

examples.title: List services that failed
examples.explain: A quick health check after boot.

examples.title: Restart a service
examples.explain: Stops then starts it, e.g. after editing its config file.
examples.warning: Interrupts the service. Restarting sshd or a network service on a remote machine can cut off your own connection.

examples.title: Start at boot and start now
examples.explain: enable creates boot-time links; --now also starts it immediately.
examples.warning: Changes boot configuration as root. Disable again with sudo systemctl disable --now <service>.

name: journalctl
summary: Read the systemd journal: logs from services, the kernel and boots.

install.note: Only where systemd-journald runs. Elsewhere logs are usually plain files in /var/log/ (e.g. /var/log/syslog, /var/log/messages) or only kernel messages via dmesg.

compat: Without root you may only see your own user's logs. Members of the systemd-journal or adm group (depending on distribution) can read the system journal; add yourself only if you understand that grants access to all logs.

examples.title: Logs of one service from the current boot
examples.explain: Opens in a pager: press / to search, G for the end, q to quit.
examples.output: Each line: timestamp, host, process[PID]: message. 'No journal files were found' or missing lines usually means you lack permission; try with sudo or check your groups.

examples.title: Follow new log lines live
examples.explain: Like tail -f for the journal. Plug in a USB device in another window and watch. Ctrl+C stops.

examples.title: Only errors (and worse) from this boot
examples.explain: Priorities from most to least severe: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug.

examples.title: Kernel messages with readable timestamps
examples.explain: Like dmesg, but persistent across reboots if the journal is stored on disk. Use -b -1 for the previous boot.
options: Start time, e.g. '2024-05-01 10:00' or '1 hour ago'

examples.title: Read the system journal with root
examples.explain: Prints the last 50 lines directly, useful for pasting into a bug report (remove secrets first).
examples.warning: Runs as root to read all logs. Logs can contain hostnames, user names and tokens; review before sharing.
options: Print directly instead of opening a pager

name: dmesg
summary: Print the kernel ring buffer: driver, USB, disk and boot messages from the kernel.
compat: Many distributions set kernel.dmesg_restrict=1, so dmesg without root fails with 'Operation not permitted'; use sudo dmesg or journalctl -k (if allowed). BusyBox dmesg lacks -T, -w and --level. The buffer is a fixed-size ring: old messages are lost.

examples.title: Recent kernel messages with human-readable times
examples.explain: Shows the last 30 lines. Your driver's printk/pr_info/dev_err output appears here.
examples.warning: Uses sudo only to read the log (needed when dmesg_restrict=1). -T times can drift after suspend/resume.
examples.output: The number in [brackets] or the time is when it was logged. Look for lines naming your device, driver, 'error', 'failed' or a call trace.

examples.title: Watch new kernel messages live
examples.explain: Keep it open while you insmod a module or plug in hardware. Ctrl+C stops.
examples.warning: Uses sudo only to read the kernel log.
options: Wait for and print new messages

examples.title: Only warnings and errors
examples.explain: Filters out the large volume of info messages.
examples.warning: Uses sudo only to read the kernel log.
options: Comma-separated levels: emerg, alert, crit, err, warn, notice, info, debug

examples.title: Search kernel messages for a driver or device
examples.explain: e.g. usb, tty, i2c or your module name. -i ignores case.
examples.warning: sudo applies only to dmesg; grep runs as you.
